title: Stack a baby's rocking ring-stacker toy: all five rings onto its tapered post in size order, largest at the bottom
instruction: Stack all five rings on the toy's post in order of size, the largest at the bottom and the smallest at the top, and leave the toy standing upright.
context: A ring-stacking toy is in most homes with a baby, and stacking its rings in size order is a standard developmental milestone (the North Carolina Early Learning and Development Progressions list "stacks five circular rings in correct size order" at about two years); parents and carers put it back together all the time. The skill is judging size and order: the rings have to go onto a tapered post in order of size, largest first; a ring put on too early sits too high on the taper and the larger rings can no longer get under it. Four of the five rings are wider than the hand opens, so each is taken by its wall, threaded over the post's ball top and dropped onto a light toy that rocks when knocked. Unlike hanging an ornament by its hook, nothing here is hooked: the order is the task.
setup: Station table, one fixed layout (x forward from the arms, y to the left, in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases). Toy: a five-ring rocking stacker matching these sizes (for example Fisher-Price Rock-a-Stack, classic 5-ring version), polypropylene, 196 mm tall, 235 g in all. Base (blue): 125 mm across and 25 mm tall, a 13 mm straight wall on a rocking dome 12 mm deep (169 mm radius of curvature); with the post 115 g, centre of mass 10 mm above the bottom; standing free at x 30, y 0. Post (yellow): a cone from 60 mm across at the base's top to 32 mm across 155 mm up, with a 32 mm ball on top. Rings: five hollow plastic rings, each 30 mm tall, flat on the table (on another edition the colours differ; go by size): red 124 mm across / 63 mm hole, 30 g, centred at x 38, y 19; orange 114 / 57.5 mm, 27 g, at x 22, y -19; yellow 105 / 52 mm, 24 g, at x 22, y 17; green 95 / 46.5 mm, 21 g, at x 40, y -18; blue 89 / 41 mm, 18 g, at x 15, y 1. Each ring's hole is 3 mm wider than the post at its own place in the stack (the red on the base, each next ring on the one below), so a ring alone on the post stops about 15 mm short of its place. Both arms start in their ready pose.
scoring: Scored every control step from the toy's and rings' positions; the score at the end of the trial counts. A ring counts as stacked when the post goes through its hole, its axis is within 10 degrees of the post's, it rests at its own place (the red within 5 mm of the base's top, each next ring within 5 mm of the top of the next larger one, measured with a ruler), neither gripper is within 5 mm of it, and the toy is upright (post within 10 degrees of vertical, on a photo). Rings are counted from the bottom in size order (red, orange, yellow, green, blue), stopping at the first that is not stacked. 1.0: all five stacked, both grippers at least 2 cm from the toy and every ring, and nothing moving more than 2 mm, held for 1 s (20 control steps in a row). 0.75: all five stacked but not yet so for 1 s. Otherwise 0.15 for each ring counted (0 to 0.6). A ring stacked above a missing or out-of-order ring earns nothing.
reset_notes: Take the rings off and lay them flat at their marks; stand the toy at its mark. Nothing is consumed.
fidelity: Rigid bodies at the toy's size and mass; every effect is PhysX contact, friction and gravity. Rings are 20-sided, square in section (real ones are rounded); the cone is 31 stacked 5 mm cylinders, so a ring stops on a 0.9 mm step. The rocking dome touches the table through a true 169 mm-radius sphere welded to the base that collides with nothing else; angular damping (1.5/s) stands in for rolling resistance. Ring heights, holes, cone and mass split are estimates; friction 0.45/0.35.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (worked at the red ring but put no ring on the post in 2,400 steps); demo: 1.0 (full score at step 1,149; the episode ended on success at step 1,168)
